result.summary: The Chorus prays for help as Orestes' old nurse Cilissa goes to fetch Aegisthus, grieving over the false news of Orestes' death. The Chorus persuades her to tell Aegisthus to come alone and unguarded, then prays to Zeus and Hermes. Aegisthus arrives, doubtful, and goes to question the strangers.

scenes.title: Chorus prays for aid
scenes.summary: The Chorus calls on the earth, Persuasion and Hermes to help Orestes, then sees the nurse approaching.
scenes.stakes: The plot to kill Aegisthus could fail if the Chorus cannot help Orestes.

scenes.title: The nurse and the message
scenes.summary: Cilissa laments Orestes' death and her years of nursing him. The Chorus secretly persuades her to tell Aegisthus to come alone.
scenes.stakes: If Aegisthus comes with his guards, Orestes' plan to kill him would fail.

scenes.title: Chorus prays to Zeus
scenes.summary: The Chorus asks Zeus and Hermes to bless the deed and urges Orestes to be brave.
scenes.stakes: The house's freedom from the curse of old murders depends on Orestes' deed succeeding.

scenes.title: Aegisthus arrives
scenes.summary: Aegisthus doubts the report of Orestes' death. The Chorus sends him in to question the strangers himself.
scenes.stakes: Aegisthus risks walking unguarded to his death.

alias_notes.explanation: Hermes is named by his mother.
The nurse is named Cilissa by the Chorus.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim the Chorus uses to trick the nurse.
Vivid, humane account of a nurse's labor with a baby.

analysis.text: The scene turns on deception: false news of death lures Aegisthus, while the nurse's grief shows the human cost of the cycle of vengeance.
The nurse's humble speech shows the Greek tragic stage giving voice to servants and everyday domestic life.

fun_facts.text: Cilissa's name means 'the Cilician woman', suggesting a foreign-born slave.

language_notes.text: The barrow is the burial mound of Agamemnon, commander of the Greek fleet at Troy, murdered by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Hermes of the nether world: Hermes guided the dead and was a god of trickery, so he is invoked to aid the secret killing.
"Unhired companion" means grief, which attends her unpaid and unasked.
Cilissa says Clytemnestra hid real laughter behind a pretended gloom before the servants.
"Children's young inwards work their own relief" means a baby's bowels relieve themselves; the nurse must guess its needs.
"I trow" means "I believe"; "office" means duty or task.
A proverb-like saying: a message told by a messenger can be set right, so the Chorus wants Aegisthus to come without guards.
"Ill wind to change" is a nautical image: Zeus may turn their bad fortune to good.
"They who rightly desire the rule of order" means those loyal to justice and lawful rule, here the supporters of Orestes against the usurpers.
The orphaned colt is Orestes, son of the dead Agamemnon; the chariot-race image pictures his dangerous task as a course to be run.
The mighty cavern is probably Apollo's oracle at Delphi, whose god commanded Orestes to avenge his father.
Maia's son is Hermes, guide of the dead, god of stealth and messenger of the gods; he is invoked to help the secret deed.
"When the wind sits fair" is a sailors' idiom for favourable fortune; the women's joyful cry is contrasted with the shrill lament.
"Baneful but offenceless deed" is a paradox: the killing is deadly, yet guiltless because justice demands it.
Perseus slew the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turned men to stone; Orestes is urged to show similar daring against a terrible foe.
'Tis startling tidings: archaic contraction and plural noun; 'tidings' means news. Aegisthus says he came because a messenger summoned him.
'Burthen' is an old form of 'burden'; 'galled' means made sore by rubbing or chafing.
The 'former murder' is Agamemnon's killing, committed by Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, which still troubles the house.
'Leaps aloft to die away in nothingness' describes a rumor flaring up like a flame or spark and then vanishing.
'Put him to the proof' means test or cross-examine him to see whether his account holds up.
'Open-eyed' means watchful and not easily deceived.

context_notes.text: Cilissa is Orestes' old nurse, who raised him after his mother sent him away as a child.
Clytemnestra has told the nurse to fetch Aegisthus, her partner and co-ruler, after the false news of Orestes' death.
The house of Atreus has a long history of murders and curses, including Atreus' feast served to his brother Thyestes.
Zeus, king of the Olympian gods, guards justice and oaths, so the Chorus appeals to him first. Orestes has secretly come to avenge Agamemnon.
The woman is Clytemnestra, Orestes' mother, who murdered Agamemnon. The Chorus urges Orestes to hold firm when she appeals to him as her son.
Aegisthus is Clytemnestra's lover and co-murderer of Agamemnon, now ruling Argos as tyrant. The Chorus, captive women of the house, have sent for him.
The Chorus, following Orestes' plan and Cilissa's advice, has told Aegisthus to come without his bodyguard, though that detail is not stated in this scene.

literary_notes.text: The Chorus calls on Persuasion and Hermes as in prayer, turning the plot of deceit into a religious act.
Clytemnestra's secret joy contrasts with her public mourning, and the news that delights her will lead to her ruin.
The nurse compares an infant to a dumb beast, using homely detail that makes her devotion realistic.
The Chorus gives the nurse a harmless-sounding reason, hiding the plot to lure Aegisthus to his death.
The cryptic remark hints that divine will is at work and that Orestes lives.
Orestes is figured as a young colt yoked to a chariot, conveying his youth, vulnerability and the strain of his task.
Murder is made an aged parent who begets offspring in the house, showing how one killing breeds further bloodshed.
Darkness and light, gloom and freedom, contrast the house's suffering with its hoped-for deliverance.
"Maia's son" names Hermes by his parentage, and the following lines describe his ambiguous, darkening speech, which suits secret deeds.
Rumor is pictured as something that leaps up and dies, and Aegisthus dismisses women's talk as insubstantial.
The Chorus's advice sounds like honest counsel, but it is a ruse to lure Aegisthus inside to his death.
Aegisthus boasts he cannot be deceived, while the audience knows the strangers are Orestes and Pylades, and he is walking into a trap.
